found.gaps:
I found no recording of a running Jumo 211 that is both clearly real and under a free licence.

No Jumo 211 appears to have been run in public recently:
- FHCAM's Ju 87 (the article calls it an R-2, wk.nr. 5709): its Jumo 211 was overhauled by Vintage V-12s in Tehachapi. The airframe moved to The Roost in Bentonville, Arkansas on 27 June 2025, and no engine run is reported.
- The American Heritage Museum's Ju 87D-5: its September 2026 update mentions no engine run.
- The Wings Museum (UK) Jumo 211 for Bodø: it only turns over by hand.
- 'White 1', mentioned in a June 2025 forum post, is FHCAM's Fw 190 D-13, which has a Jumo 213, not a 211.

So the Bf 109 stand-ins are the strongest leads. All of them still need their licence checked on the blocked pages (Freesound and Commons), and a Freesound 'Sampling+' or a Commons CC BY-SA licence would rule a file out.

I could not read any YouTube page; every fetch was rate-limited or failed. These titles are unverified for content and CC licence:
- 'Jumo 211 Motor - Engine' https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YhjdC4Yt6l0
- 'Junkers Jumo engine of a JU 88 bomber' https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=woX6OWRiXHI
- 'Ju-87 start engine' https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XWnr-5rZ5gM
- 'Junkers Jumo 211' https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RacYSErVi1s

None is confirmed to show an engine running, and several Jumo results were slideshows, simulator or RC-model videos.

I found no free-licence in-flight DB 605 recording. The best-known flying DB 605 Bf 109s are 'Red 7' G-4 D-FWME and Messerschmitt Stiftung G-6 D-FMBB, and they only turned up as photos or videos of unknown licence.

Deliberately excluded:
- UAH Archives 'World War II Aircraft: Heinkel HE-111 (German) (Interior)' (https://archives.uah.edu/repositories/2/archival_objects/93528). It is a genuine wartime He 111 recording, but the page lists its source as BBC Sound Effects (EC 500E), it has no licence, and it can only be heard in the reading room.
- craigsmith 'G04-07-WWII Stuka engine drone' (https://freesound.org/people/craigsmith/sounds/437771/): an excluded library series.
- Mastersoundboy2005 Stuka siren/scream clips, Sphyrna 'stuka01.mp3' (https://freesound.org/people/Sphyrna/sounds/69189/) and Farepello 'diveBomber.WAV' (https://freesound.org/people/Farepello/sounds/792800/): origin not shown, and they are likely designed or taken from films.
- YleArkisto 'Junkers, a 1936 model, taking off' (https://freesound.org/people/YleArkisto/sounds/256042/): almost certainly not a Jumo 211 (the aircraft type isn't named).
- DVIDS 'Junkers Ju 88D-1/Trop' video (https://www.dvidshub.net/video/1019037/junkers-ju-88d-1-trop): almost certainly a static museum exhibit with narration, not an engine run (snippet only).
- DVIDS audio 'ISR Tour Bf 109G-10' (https://www.dvidshub.net/audio/41601/isr-tour-bf-109g-10): seemingly a museum audio-tour item, not an engine recording (snippet only).
- AWM field recordings are CC BY-NC 3.0 AU and genuine (Richard Johnson, 2014), but they hold no German aircraft.

Next step: the owner should open the Freesound and Commons pages to confirm licence, length and whether other aircraft or crowds are audible. They could also contact FHCAM or Vintage V-12s for any Jumo 211 test-cell recording.

leads.title: HMAS Oxley, Oberon class submarine - operational sounds (segment 24: "Torpedo Room - Firing torpedo")
leads.site: Australian War Memorial collection (awm.gov.au), accession S04697
leads.licence: CC BY-NC (3.0 AU)
leads.licence_evidence: The page says "Item copyright: © Australian War Memorial" and "This item is licensed under CC BY-NC", with a CC badge linking to CC BY-NC 3.0 AU. It also says "Only personal, non-commercial, research and study use permitted".
leads.what: A real recording made aboard the RAN Oberon-class submarine HMAS Oxley, about 1980, by Defence Public Relations (DPR). The original is a DAT tape (48 kHz, 16-bit, stereo) lasting 1 hr 16 min. It has 24 listed segments: ward room, bridge, periscope depth, klaxon alarms, sonar, an underwater cavitating propeller, and as segment 24, "Torpedo Room - Firing torpedo". The page has a single MP3 of the whole tape: https://s3-ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/awm-media/collection/S04697/audio/3849992.MP3. Recording location and microphone placement are not stated.
leads.fit: This is the only lead found that is a real torpedo tube firing on a real submarine. The Oberon class used 21-inch tubes, close to WW2 submarine practice. It would give the tube's discharge and air impulse from inside the boat.
leads.concerns: It is heard from inside the torpedo room, so there is no outside splash. Its timecode inside the 76-minute MP3 is not given, but it is listed last, so it is probably near the end. The access copy is an MP3. The AWM labels the object type "Sound Effect", although it is a DPR field recording from a real boat; check that nothing was edited or layered. There may be crew talk or orders around the shot. The licence is non-commercial, which suits a personal game.

leads.what: About 5 hours of audio in 168 WAV files, recorded with a Brüel & Kjær 8104 hydrophone 2.5 m deep at the centre of an 8 x 5 x 5 m anechoic tank at Lisbon Naval Base. leads.concerns: The licence must be confirmed on Figshare before use. Some files deliberately include transients (metal-tube impacts, air-rifle shots) and noise (bubbling, hoses, bucket pours), so pick files with codes T00 and N00. It is a tank, not open water. verdicts.reason: torpedo_launch, segment 24. I read the page and it backs the claims: "HMAS Oxley, Oberon class submarine - operational sounds", S04697, maker Defence Public Relations (DPR), c1980, "digital audio tape (DAT); AGFA DA 120; 48kHz; 16 bit; stereo", 1 hr 16 min. Segment 24 is "Torpedo Room - Firing torpedo". Licence text: "This item is licensed under CC BY-NC" (linked to 3.0 AU) and "Only personal, non-commercial, research and study use permitted". The MP3 link is real: HTTP 200, 17,256,549 bytes, last modified 14 Mar 2018. Two things the searcher missed. (1) The online copy is much worse than the DAT spec. Its frame header reads MPEG-2 Layer III, 22.05 kHz, MONO, with a Xing VBR header, and the file size works out to an average of about 30 kbps over 76 minutes. So nothing above about 11 kHz survives, and the 48 kHz stereo master is not online. (2) DAT did not exist in 1980, so the DAT is a later transfer of an older tape. The page does not say whether segments were edited. Object type "Sound Effect" does not mean a commercial library, because the maker is the RAN's own PR unit aboard a named boat. Still listen for layering. Other limits: it is heard inside the torpedo room, so there is no outside splash. Crew orders are likely close by (segments 22-23 are "speed and direction orders"). leads.what: Times of underwater explosions automatically detected in real hydrophone recordings from the Olympic Coast sanctuary site OC02_04 (about 48.49 N, 125.00 W), 13 July to 1 Oct 2020. leads.fit: These are real distant underwater explosions on a fixed hydrophone with no music or talk, which matches the 'distant underwater explosions' part of the sound.
leads.concerns: The records do not say what caused the explosions; they could be small seal bombs, not large charges. Using them means downloading large raw recordings and cutting out each event by its timestamp. The detector ran on audio decimated to 12 kHz (the archived originals may have a higher rate). The licence conflict should be checked with NCEI (ncei.info@noaa.gov).

found.gaps: I found no public-domain or Creative Commons hydrophone recording of a real ship sinking or breaking up. The closest real recordings are CTBTO hydroacoustic detections of the container ship MOL Comfort breaking in two and sinking (2013, station HA08; https://conferences.ctbto.org/event/30/contributions/5604/) and a probable El Faro sinking signal (2015, station HA10; https://conferences.ctbto.org/event/7/contributions/879/). Both are conference posters only. No audio was released, and CTBTO reuse terms are unknown; the owner could email the authors. I found no hydrophone recording of any artificial-reef sinking (Oriskany, Vandenberg, Radford, SS United States). The SS United States (sunk 2026 by flooding, no explosives) has only YouTube news or third-party videos with unknown licences. For the Oriskany I found only a military.com video credited to 'MLT Staff' with an unknown licence (https://military.com/video/logistics-and-supplies/naval-equipment/navy-eod-sinks-uss-oriskany-with-c4/3102218807001) and a DVIDS feature 'The Great Carrier Reef' (https://www.dvidshub.net/video/346083/great-carrier-reef), which is probably edited with music or narration. The NOAA PMEL multimedia page and the Ocean Explorer sound gallery have no explosion or sinking clips. PMEL does have a real hydrophone recording of an iceberg running aground (https://pmel.noaa.gov/acoustics/multimedia/Iceberglng-lowfre.mov). It is NOAA work with no licence stated, and is only a possible stand-in for low grinding or settling, not a ship. The Duke Sonic Dictionary 'Wreck' (https://sonicdictionary.duke.edu/items/wreck.html, page read, CC BY-NC 4.0, 3:03, Sam Pickerill, 2015, hydrophone over a sunken 70-ft tanker off Jupiter Island FL) is real and properly licensed. It is only wreck-site ambience, not a sinking, so I left it out of the leads. Freesound searches turned up only effects-library or designed items (craigsmith G and R series, a 'stereotypical sinking submarine sound') or unrelated hydrophone water recordings. DOSITS pages have no audio clips and are marked 'All rights reserved'. All DVIDS pages, and the YouTube pages (rate-limited), still need the owner to check three things: whether the clip has natural sound or music, the rights line, and the length. I used navy.mil and dover.af.mil pages only where they appeared in search results, never by building URLs from DVIDS IDs. Delaware DNREC (Shearwater, https://youtu.be/omhTQg1Sow0) and NJ.com (Tamaroa, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=itzAWOwbyeQ) reef-sinking videos exist, but their licences are unknown, so I left them out.

verdicts.rule_broken: None of the hard rules is clearly broken. I am rejecting it on fit and appropriateness.
verdicts.reason: I read the USCG Titan page (https://www.news.uscg.mil/News-by-Region/Headquarters/Titan-Submersible/). It confirms a NOAA moored passive acoustic recorder about 900 miles away captured 'the suspected acoustic signature of the Titan submersible implosion, June 18, 2023'. It also says NOAA 'approved its use in the investigation and public release', and it has a 'Download it here' link to a DVIDS item with this title. The page names no licence and says nothing about speed-up or filtering. I did not see the numeric ID 951839, and DVIDS is blocked, so the rights line is unread. Even if the licence is public domain, this is a weak lead. It is one implosion of a small submersible, not a ship going down or settling, and it was heard from about 900 miles away. Whether the clip was sped up or filtered for release is unknown. It is also the recorded death of five people, which most owners would not want as a game effect. A real SINKEX or reef scuttling covers the same need without these problems.

I read the page. It matches the claim: title 'Pacific Fleet forces conduct SINKEX as part of Large Scale Exercise 2021', dated 15 Aug 2021, 1:26, source Commander, U.S. Pacific Fleet, credited '(U.S. Navy and Marine Corps video)'. It is a US government work on an official .mil site, so public domain, though the page has no explicit rights line. The page does not mention natural sound, music or narration. The owner should download it and check for real sound before relying on it.

I read the page. It states the licence as CC0 1.0. It also lists access level 'non-public' and rights 'otherRestrictions' without explanation, yet it links public data. The raw WAVs have to be fetched from the NCEI/Google Cloud archive and each event cut out by its timestamp. The page does not say what caused the explosions: 'explosive sounds' were matched against a template. At sanctuary sites they may well be small fishery seal bombs, which would be short pops, nothing like a ship-sized blast. Keep it as the one lead with a clean licence and certainly real sound, but expect small, distant events.

My web-search budget was used up, so I could not re-run title searches. I checked leads by reading the pages that are not blocked: navy.mil, dover.af.mil, news.uscg.mil, catalog.data.gov and scubaboard. The searcher was told to try these but returned nothing from them:

Agencies often put cameras or hydrophones on board.
(2) NOAA PMEL Acoustics program sound pages, and the wider NOAA NCEI passive-acoustic archive beyond SanctSound (e.g. the Ocean Noise Reference Stations). Also NOAA's own SanctSound pages, which may offer ready-cut example clips of explosions.
(3) USGS or university acoustic labs (e.g. Scripps, WHOI, URI's DOSITS audio gallery; licences vary and need checking).
(4) Ocean Networks Canada hydrophone archive (data under CC BY), for any recorded scuttling or underwater blast in BC waters.
(5) Other DVIDS SINKEX B-roll, searched by exercise rather than generic title, e.g. RIMPAC 2024 and RIMPAC 2022 sinking exercises, plus Valiant Shield SINKEXs. Unedited B-roll is the likeliest to carry natural sound. Search-snippet only, for the owner's computer to read.
(6) Wikimedia Commons categories of US Navy SINKEX or ship-sinking video files (public domain; blocked here, so search-snippet only).
(7) Freesound field recordists' CC0 or CC BY hydrophone recordings of real underwater blasts, such as demolition or blast-fishing research recordings. Exclude craigsmith G/R/S uploads and packs. Blocked here, so search-snippet only.
(8) For the 'hull settling or groaning' half of the need, real hydrophone recordings of wrecks or scuttled hulls from NOAA sanctuary wreck surveys (e.g. Thunder Bay, Stellwagen Bank). None of the current leads covers creaking or settling, only blasts and impacts.

leads.title: Mortar - operational sounds (AWM accession S04685)
leads.licence: CC BY-NC (3.0 AU)
leads.licence_evidence: Page states: 'This item is licensed under CC BY-NC'. It also says 'Item copyright: © Australian War Memorial' and 'Only personal, non-commercial, research and study use permitted', which fits a personal, non-commercial game.
leads.what: A field recording of mortar fire made by Defence Public Relations (DPR) at Singleton, New South Wales, about 1968. The description has two notes: 'concentrated mortar fire and explosions' and 'mortar fire and explosions with and without orders'. Length 6 min 34 s. It is held as a DAT transfer (48 kHz, 16-bit, stereo). No individual recordist is named and mic placement is not stated.
leads.fit: It is a real army recording of mortars firing at a real range, and part of it is described as firing without spoken orders. The thump of the tube firing is the closest land equivalent to a depth-charge projector. The licence is clean for non-commercial use.
leads.concerns: The AWM files it under object type 'Sound Effect', but it is a DPR field recording, not a commercial effects library. Explosions are mixed in, and some passages have fire orders shouted over them. Distance to the mortar is not stated. The page did not show whether the audio can be streamed or downloaded, or in what quality.

leads.title: Operational sounds of United States military aircraft, armour and weapons used during the war in Vietnam, 1962-1972 (AWM S03297), track 16 'Close-up of mortar firing'
leads.licence: CC BY-NC (3.0 AU)
leads.licence_evidence: Page states: 'This item is licensed under CC BY-NC' (Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 3.0 Australia), with 'Item copyright: © Australian War Memorial'.
leads.what: A 1 hr 4 min compilation on a 1/4-inch tape reel, mono, labelled as Vietnam-era US military sounds. Track 16 is 'Close-up of mortar firing' and track 5 includes mortar fire during a firefight. The maker and recording date are unknown. It came to the AWM through the AWM Research Grants Scheme.
leads.fit: It is the only item found that is explicitly labelled as a close-up mortar firing, which matches the close-by thump the game needs.
leads.concerns: The origin is unclear: no maker is named, and the reel includes out-of-context items such as a cheering crowd and a teletype. It may have been copied from a commercial effects record, which would break the no-library rule. The owner should check its provenance before using it. Track 16's length is not given, and the audio is mono tape.

leads.title: 'Raid on Berlin': actuality recording of an RAF bombing raid over Berlin, 4 September 1943, recorded in Lancaster 'F' Freddy of 207 Squadron (AWM S00199)
leads.licence: Public domain
leads.licence_evidence: Page states: 'Item copyright: Copyright expired - public domain' and marks the item with the Public Domain Mark 1.0. The same page also carries a boilerplate line ('Copyright restrictions apply. Only personal, non-commercial... use permitted') that contradicts this. A personal, non-commercial game satisfies either reading.
leads.what: A real recording made aboard Lancaster ED586 EM-F of 207 Squadron RAF during the raid on Berlin of 4 September 1943. Sound recordist Reginald Pidsley; BBC war correspondent Wynford Vaughan-Thomas narrates. The listed segments are arriving over Berlin, preparing to bomb, evading searchlights, releasing the bomb load, a night-fighter attack and the return fire. The page says the sudden upward lurch of the aircraft at release drove the recording needle through the acetate into the aluminium, leaving a noise artefact. Length 6 min 32 s, from a 78 rpm disc, mono.
leads.fit: It is a genuine WW2 heavy-bomber bomb release recorded in the aircraft, from the war the game is set in. It is the only lead found with the real release moment inside the aircraft.
leads.concerns: Vaughan-Thomas talks over most of it, and crew intercom is present. Right at the release there is a needle-gouge artefact. It is 1943 disc audio with limited fidelity and surface noise. It is a BBC radio actuality broadcast, not the BBC Sound Effects library, but the owner should be aware of the BBC origin.
